items.explanationShort:
librairie (FR) = a bookstore.
library (EN) = a place where you borrow books.
French sells books; English lends them.

actuellement (FR) = currently, at the present time.
actually (EN) = in fact, really, contrary to what was expected.
French speaks about time; English corrects a statement.

éventuellement (FR) = possibly, perhaps.
eventually (EN) = in the end, after some time.
French is uncertainty; English is outcome.

collège (FR) = middle school (ages 11-15).
college (EN) = higher education after high school.
Teenagers in French, adults in English.

location (FR) = a rental (flat, car, equipment).
location (EN) = a place or position.
Renting in French, place in English.

stage (FR) = an internship or training period.
stage (EN) = a platform for performances, or a phase.
Work experience in French, theatre in English.

chair (FR) = flesh, the soft tissue of the body.
chair (EN) = a seat or piece of furniture.
French is flesh; English is furniture.

caméra (FR) = a device mainly used to record video.
camera (EN) = a device used to take photographs or record images.
French usually distinguishes photo ('appareil photo') and video ('caméra'); English often uses 'camera' for both.

préservatif (FR) = a condom.
preservative (EN) = a chemical added to food to keep it fresh.
A notorious source of confusion for travellers ordering food in France.

raisin (FR) = a grape.
raisin (EN) = a dried grape.
French is fresh; English is dried.

tissu (FR) = fabric or cloth.
tissue (EN) = thin disposable paper, or biological body tissue in science.
Both from Old French 'tissu' (woven); the meanings split between textile and paper.

monnaie (FR) = coins, change, or currency in circulation.
money (EN) = money in general, including cash or wealth.
French counts the change; English counts the wealth.

pétrole (FR) = crude oil in its natural state.
petrol (EN) = gasoline used as fuel in cars.
French names the raw oil; English names the fuel.

grappe (FR) = a cluster or bunch, especially of fruit on a stem.
grape (EN) = a single small fruit used for eating or making wine.
French names the whole bunch hanging together; English names the individual berry.

définitivement (FR) = permanently, for good.
definitely (EN) = certainly, without doubt.
Permanent in French, certain in English.

assister (FR) = to attend or be present at an event.
assist (EN) = to help someone.
From Latin 'assistere' (to stand by); French kept the passive witness sense, English took the active help sense.

attendre (FR) = to wait.
attend (EN) = to be present at an event.
From Latin 'attendere' (to stretch toward); French kept the waiting, English kept the showing up.

demander (FR) = to ask.
demand (EN) = to insist on receiving something.
French asks; English insists.

quitter (FR) = to leave a place or a person.
quit (EN) = to stop doing something, especially a job or a habit.
French leaves; English stops.

avertir (FR) = to warn or notify someone in advance.
avert (EN) = to prevent or turn away from danger.
French warns first; English blocks danger.

blesser (FR) = to injure or wound someone.
bless (EN) = to give a holy or divine favour.
French injures; English blesses.

charger (FR) = to load something or charge a battery.
charge (EN) = to ask for payment or accuse someone.
Some overlap exists, but French usually means to load.

sort (FR) = goes out, comes out, gets out; as a noun, it can also mean fate or a spell.
sort (EN) = to classify, arrange, or put into order.
French can mean coming out or fate; English puts things in order.

médecin (FR) = a doctor, the person who treats patients.
medicine (EN) = a drug or substance used to treat illness.
Same Latin root 'medicus,' but French named the healer while English named the remedy.

lecture (FR) = reading.
lecture (EN) = a talk or spoken presentation.
French reads; English speaks.

journal (FR) = a newspaper or TV news bulletin.
journal (EN) = a diary or academic publication.
French reports the news; English records it.

cave (FR) = a cellar or basement, often used for wine.
cave (EN) = a natural underground cavern.
French stores wine; English explores rock caves.

habit (FR) = a piece of clothing, or clothes in general.
habit (EN) = a repeated behaviour or routine.
From Latin 'habitus' which covered both dress and condition; each language picked one meaning.

travail (FR) = work or labour.
travel (EN) = going on a journey.
French works; English moves.

coin (FR) = a corner or a spot.
coin (EN) = a small metal disc used as money.
French 'coin' comes from Latin 'cuneus' (wedge), describing the angular shape of a corner.

phrase (FR) = a full sentence.
phrase (EN) = a group of words, not always a full sentence.
French is complete; English can be shorter.

chat (FR) = a cat.
chat (EN) = an online written conversation.
French purrs; English messages.

supporter (FR) = to tolerate or endure something unpleasant.
support (EN) = to help, encourage, or hold something up.
French endures; English helps.

résumer (FR) = to summarize or condense.
resume (EN) = to continue after a pause.
French shortens; English starts again.

actuel (FR) = current, present-day.
actual (EN) = real, true, not imagined.
French is current; English is real.

préjudice (FR) = harm or damage, especially in legal contexts.
prejudice (EN) = a biased opinion formed without evidence.
Latin 'praejudicium' (prior judgment) split into legal harm in French and personal bias in English.

assumer (FR) = to take responsibility for something, to own it.
assume (EN) = to suppose or take for granted.
French owns it; English guesses it.

prétendre (FR) = to claim or assert something as true.
pretend (EN) = to fake or act as if something is true when it is not.
French claims; English fakes.

adresser (FR) = to send or direct something to someone.
address (EN) = to deal with a problem or issue.
Some overlap exists, but French usually means to send or direct.

délai (FR) = a time limit or allowed period.
delay (EN) = lateness or postponement.
French gives you time; English makes you late.

étiquette (FR) = a label or price tag.
etiquette (EN) = rules of polite behaviour.
French sticks on objects; English guides behaviour.

engager (FR) = to hire someone or commit yourself.
engage (EN) = to involve, attract attention, or take part.
French hires; English grabs attention.

formation (FR) = training or education.
formation (EN) = an arrangement or structure of things.
French trains people; English arranges things.

fournir (FR) = to supply or provide.
furnish (EN) = to equip with furniture.
French provides; English decorates.

éventuel (FR) = possible, potential, not certain.
eventual (EN) = final, happening at the end, ultimate.
French is uncertainty; English is end result.

journée (FR) = the span of a full day.
journey (EN) = a trip from one place to another.
French refers to a day; English refers to travel.

rester (FR) = to stay or remain somewhere.
rest (EN) = to relax or stop working.
French stays; English relaxes.

sympathique (FR) = nice, friendly, pleasant.
sympathetic (EN) = showing compassion or understanding.
French is friendly; English shows compassion.

sensible (FR) = sensitive, easily affected emotionally.
sensible (EN) = usually practical, reasonable, showing good judgment.
In everyday use, French is about feeling; English is about judgment. Rare literary/legal uses overlap, so this is a practical trap.

envie (FR) = a desire or craving for something.
envy (EN) = jealousy of what others have.
Wanting chocolate is French 'envie'; resenting someone else's chocolate is English 'envy.'

déception (FR) = disappointment, when expectations are not met.
deception (EN) = trickery, deliberate lying or misleading.
French is about unmet hopes; English is about intentional dishonesty.

décevoir (FR) = to disappoint someone.
deceive (EN) = to trick or mislead someone.
French hurts feelings; English breaks trust.

roman (FR) = a novel, a work of fiction.
roman (EN) = relating to ancient Rome.
French names the story; English names the empire.

bras (FR) = an arm, the body part.
brass (EN) = a yellow metal alloy.
One moves; the other shines.

limonade (FR) = a fizzy lemon soda.
lemonade (EN) = a still drink made with lemon juice.
In France it bubbles; in English it does not.

prune (FR) = a fresh plum.
prune (EN) = a dried plum.
French is fresh; English is dried.

pain (FR) = bread.
pain (EN) = physical or emotional suffering.
Same spelling, totally different meaning.

sale (FR) = dirty, filthy.
sale (EN) = a discount event, or the act of selling.
Unrelated roots: French from Frankish (dirty), English from Old Norse (selling).

table (FR) = table, the furniture.
table (EN) = the same piece of furniture.
Same word, but English says it more like TAY-b'l; French keeps the final syllable clearer.

orange (FR) = the fruit and the colour.
orange (EN) = the same fruit and colour.
A safe transparent word, with stress on the first syllable in English: OR-inj.

chocolat (FR) = chocolate.
chocolate (EN) = the same cacao-based food.
The spelling stays close, but English often compresses the middle: CHOK-lut.

fruit (FR) = fruit.
fruit (EN) = fruit.
Perfectly transparent, but pronunciation changes: English sounds like FROOT, not a French-style 'frui'.

restaurant (FR) = a place where meals are served.
restaurant (EN) = the same place.
Borrowed from French, but English usually pronounces the final consonant more clearly.

zoo (FR) = zoo.
zoo (EN) = zoo.
A fully international word. In English, stretch the 'oo' sound like a long French 'ou'.

appartement (FR) = an apartment.
apartment (EN) = a residential unit in a building.
Very close, but English drops the French '-e-ment' feel; in UK English, 'flat' is also common.

accident (FR) = an accident.
accident (EN) = an accident.
Same spelling and meaning. English puts the stress at the start: AK-si-dent.

information (FR) = information; in plural, it can also mean the news.
information (EN) = information.
Useful grammar trap: in English, 'information' is uncountable. Say 'some information,' not 'informations'.

communication (FR) = communication.
communication (EN) = communication.
The '-tion' bridge is reliable here; English stress falls late: com-mu-ni-KAY-shun.

situation (FR) = situation.
situation (EN) = situation.
A strong true friend for daily life and work. English often makes the 'tu' sound like 'tch': si-tchou-AY-shun.

solution (FR) = a solution.
solution (EN) = a solution.
Same word in business and science. English stress lands on the middle: so-LOO-shun.

nation (FR) = nation.
nation (EN) = nation.
Transparent in meaning. In English, the 'a' sounds like 'ay': NAY-shun.

important (FR) = important.
important (EN) = important.
Same meaning, different rhythm: English avoids the French nasal ending and stresses the middle.

possible (FR) = possible.
possible (EN) = possible.
The '-ible' ending is a useful bridge; English stress is on the first syllable: POS-si-b'l.

impossible (FR) = impossible.
impossible (EN) = impossible.
The negative prefix 'im-' works the same way in both languages. One pattern, many useful words.

excellent (FR) = excellent.
excellent (EN) = excellent.
Same written form, but English strongly stresses the first syllable: EK-suh-lent.

intelligent (FR) = intelligent.
intelligent (EN) = intelligent.
A real true friend. The English 'g' sounds like 'j': in-TEL-i-jent.

urgent (FR) = urgent.
urgent (EN) = urgent.
Same meaning. English starts with an 'ur' sound and often makes the 'g' soft: UR-jent.

taxi (FR) = taxi.
taxi (EN) = taxi.
The meaning travels everywhere. In English, the stress is on the first syllable: TAK-see.

bus (FR) = bus.
bus (EN) = bus.
Same everyday word, but the English vowel sounds like 'uh' or 'bus' in 'but,' not the French 'u'.

menu (FR) = menu.
menu (EN) = menu.
Borrowed from French. English often adds a small 'y' sound before the final vowel: MEN-yoo.

animal (FR) = animal.
animal (EN) = animal.
Same spelling and meaning. English stresses the first syllable: AN-i-m'l.

musique (FR) = music.
music (EN) = music.
The French '-ique' often becomes English '-ic'. Meaning stays aligned; spelling gets shorter.

culture (FR) = culture.
culture (EN) = culture.
Same core idea: arts, beliefs, habits, and cultivation. English starts with a 'kul' sound: KUL-chur.

minute (FR) = a minute of time.
minute (EN) = a minute of time.
Same time word. Extra trap: English 'minute' pronounced my-NYOOT is an adjective meaning very small.

seconde (FR) = a second of time, or second position.
second (EN) = the same time unit or position.
French adds a final '-e'; English stops at the 'd'.

public (FR) = public.
public (EN) = public.
Same idea: open to everyone or linked to people as a whole. English spelling avoids French '-que'.

total (FR) = total.
total (EN) = total.
A clean true friend for numbers and summaries. English often sounds like TOH-t'l.

normal (FR) = normal.
normal (EN) = normal.
Zero difference in meaning. English stresses the first syllable: NOR-m'l.

national (FR) = national.
national (EN) = national.
Built from 'nation' in both languages. In English, the middle sounds shorter: NASH-uh-n'l.

international (FR) = international.
international (EN) = international.
The prefix 'inter-' works the same way. In fast American English, the 't' may be softened or dropped.

valeur (FR) = worth, importance, moral principle.
value (EN) = numerical or economic amount.
French can mean importance; English usually means a quantity.

photographe (FR) = a photographer, someone who takes photographs.
photographer (EN) = a person who takes photographs.
Same profession; English adds -er at the end.

responsable (FR) = in charge or accountable.
responsible (EN) = the same: accountable or in charge.
In French the noun can also mean a manager.

danger = a risk of harm or threat to safety.
Both languages inherited the word from Old French, keeping the sense of threat.

produit = something manufactured, grown, or created for sale.
From Latin 'producere' (to bring forth), both name what is made.

organisation = a structured group of people working together.
Same meaning in both languages.

administration = the management or governance of an organization.
From Latin 'administrare' (to serve, manage), both refer to governance.

libraire (FR) = a bookseller.
librarian (EN) = a person who works in a library.
Seller in French; library staff in English.

historique (FR) = historic, significant in history.
historical (EN) = related to history in general.
French often means important; English simply relates to history.

économique = relating to the economy, trade, and production of wealth.
From Greek 'oikonomia' (household management), both kept the resource meaning.

magasin (FR) = a shop or store where you buy things.
magazine (EN) = a periodical publication with articles and photos.
Both come from Arabic 'makhazin' (storehouses); one stores goods, the other stores stories.

veste (FR) = a jacket, a garment with sleeves.
vest (EN) = a sleeveless undergarment or waistcoat.
French wears a jacket; English wears an undershirt.

réclamer (FR) = to demand or ask for something.
reclaim (EN) = to take something back or recover it.
French demands; English takes back.

formidable (FR) = wonderful or fantastic.
formidable (EN) = impressive, powerful, or intimidating.
French praises; English warns.

crier (FR) = to shout loudly.
cry (EN) = to shed tears.
French shouts; English weeps.

portrait (FR) and portrait (EN) share the same meaning: an image of a person.
The oral trap is the final sound: English pronounces the final t, while French keeps it silent.

garage means the same in both languages: a place for parking or repairing vehicles.
Pronunciation varies in English, especially between British and American accents, but the meaning stays aligned.

touriste (FR) = tourist (EN), the same traveller.
Pattern to remember: French -iste often becomes English -ist.

science means science in both languages.
The spelling is friendly, but the English sound changes: the c is silent and the i sounds like 'eye'.

architecture means architecture in both languages.
The oral trap is the ch: in English it sounds like k, as in AR-ki-tek-chur.

regarder (FR) = to look at or watch.
regard (EN) = respect or consideration.
French looks; English respects.

caution (FR) = a security deposit or bail money.
caution (EN) = care taken to avoid danger or mistakes.
French turned it into a financial guarantee; English turned it into a warning.

pet (FR) = a fart, gas released from the body.
pet (EN) = a domesticated animal kept for companionship.
Flatulence in French; furry friend in English.

patron (FR) = the boss or employer who runs the business.
patron (EN) = a loyal customer or financial supporter.
From Latin 'patronus' (protector); French took the authority side, English took the generosity side.

pièce (FR) = a room, coin, or theatrical play.
piece (EN) = a part of something.
French enters a room; English takes a part.

massage means massage in both languages.
English often keeps a French-like ending and stresses the last part of the word.

surprise means surprise in both languages.
In English, the final -se sounds like z, and the r is usually pronounced in rhotic accents.

concert means a live musical performance in both languages.
In English, the noun usually stresses the first syllable, and the final t is pronounced.

effort means effort in both languages.
The useful detail is stress: English puts the weight at the start of the word.

virus works in medicine and computing in both languages.
Pronunciation trap: the English i sounds like 'eye', as in VAI-rus.

défaut (FR) = a flaw or imperfection.
default (EN) = the preset option or a failure to pay.
French points to a flaw; English points to a preset.

physicien (FR) = a physicist, a scientist who studies physics.
physician (EN) = a medical doctor.
Same root, different worlds: physics in French, medicine in English.

propre (FR) = clean, or one's own.
proper (EN) = correct or appropriate.
French washes things; English approves them.

injure (FR) = a verbal insult or offensive word.
injury (EN) = a physical wound or bodily harm.
French wounds with words; English wounds the body.

course (FR) = an errand, a shopping trip, or a race.
course (EN) = a class, a direction, or a part of a meal.
French runs errands; English runs classes.

train is fully transparent in writing and meaning.
Pronunciation trap: English has no French nasal sound here; say a clear 'ay' sound, as in trayn.

dialogue means dialogue in both languages.
Spelling note: American English also uses the shorter form dialog, especially in computing.

costume (FR) = a men's business suit, jacket and trousers for formal wear.
costume (EN) = fancy dress, a disguise, or a stage outfit.
Boardroom in French, costume party in English.
The French suffix -iste becomes the shorter English -ist. Same role: someone who creates art. English stresses the first syllable: AR-tist.
A perfect twin in writing and meaning: a broad city street. In English, the last syllable often sounds like 'you': AV-en-you.

blanc (FR) = white, the colour.
blank (EN) = empty, unmarked, or without content.
Both from a Germanic root meaning bright or shining, but one became a colour and the other an absence.

joli (FR) = pretty or attractive in appearance.
jolly (EN) = cheerful, merry, full of good spirits.
French looks pretty; English feels cheerful.

retirer (FR) = to withdraw or remove, especially money from a bank.
retire (EN) = to stop working permanently at the end of a career.
French withdraws; English stops working.

prévenir (FR) = to warn or alert someone in advance.
prevent (EN) = to stop something from happening.
From Latin 'praevenire' (to come before); French warns before the event, English blocks it.

heurter (FR) = to bump into or collide with something.
hurt (EN) = to feel pain, or to cause someone pain.
French bumps into things; English feels pain.
Same spelling and same meaning. The oral trap is stress: English puts the weight at the start, as in SY-lence.
An international word from Italian, with the same meaning in both languages. English usually stresses the middle: pi-A-no.
Identical in writing and meaning. English stretches the ending and says it more like RAY-dee-oh.
The accent disappears in English, but the meaning stays the same. Both languages shorten it the same way: telephone becomes phone.
A key professional true friend. Same written form, same idea: a file, paper, or digital document. English stresses the first syllable: DOC-you-ment.

limon (FR) = silt, fine sediment deposited by rivers.
lemon (EN) = a sour yellow citrus fruit.
River mud in French; sour fruit in English.

carte (FR) = a map, a card, or a restaurant menu.
cart (EN) = a wheeled vehicle for carrying goods.
French reads maps; English pushes carts.

supplier (FR) = to beg or plead desperately for mercy.
supply (EN) = to provide goods or resources.
French begs; English provides.

éducation = the process of teaching, learning, and personal development.
From Latin 'educare' (to bring up, to rear), both kept the full educational meaning.

apologie (FR) = a defense or strong justification of something.
apology (EN) = saying sorry for a mistake.
Both come from Greek 'apologia' (a speech in defense), but English shifted toward regret.

village = a small rural settlement, smaller than a town.
From Old French, both name the same type of community.

station = a stopping point for transport or services.
From Latin 'statio' (a standing place), both describe where things halt.

acte/act = an action, a deed, or a division of a play.
Both also have legal uses: "acte de naissance," "Act of Parliament."
Same meaning in most everyday contexts.

parc = a public green space, or an enclosed area like a theme park.
From Old French, both kept the recreational outdoor meaning.

océan = a vast body of saltwater covering much of the Earth.
Named after the Greek titan Okeanos, who personified the world-encircling river.

assiette (FR) = a plate, a dish used for eating.
asset (EN) = a valuable resource or property.
French holds food; English holds value.

chef (FR) = a leader, boss, or head of a group.
chef (EN) = a professional cook in a restaurant.
French means a leader; English means a professional cook.

parcours (FR) = a route, path, or career journey.
parkour (EN) = an urban acrobatic sport of jumping over obstacles.
French means a route; English names a sport.

fabrique (FR) = a factory or manufacturing workshop.
fabric (EN) = textile, cloth, or woven material.
The place of making vs. what gets made.

crayon (FR) = a pencil.
crayon (EN) = a wax colouring stick.
French writes homework; English colours it.

ballet = a classical dance form performed to music.
Born in the Italian and French courts of the Renaissance, the word and art spread together unchanged.

continent = one of the Earth's major landmasses.
From Latin 'continere' (to hold together), both name the same geographical divisions.

résidence = a place where someone lives, especially a formal or official dwelling.
From Latin 'residere' (to sit back, settle), both kept the dwelling meaning.

profession = a skilled occupation requiring specialized training.
From Latin 'professio' (public declaration), both describe a declared career or trade.

émotion = a strong feeling such as joy, fear, or sadness.
From Latin 'emovere' (to stir up), both kept the inner experience meaning.

issue (FR) = an exit or way out.
issue (EN) = a problem, topic, or matter.
French leaves the room; English starts the discussion.

pull (FR) = a sweater or jumper.
pull (EN) = to draw something toward you.
French wears it; English tugs it.

billet (FR) = a ticket or banknote.
billet (EN) = temporary lodging assigned to soldiers.
French buys tickets; English houses soldiers.

attirer (FR) = to attract or draw toward.
attire (EN) = clothing or dress.
French attracts; English dresses.

robe (FR) = a dress worn by women.
robe (EN) = a gown or bathrobe.
French means a dress; English means a robe or gown.

théâtre = a venue for live performances, or the art of dramatic performance.
From Greek 'theatron' (viewing place), both kept the same dramatic meaning.

université = a higher education institution that awards degrees.
From Latin 'universitas' (community of scholars); the first ones appeared in Bologna and Paris around 1150.

page = a leaf of a book, document, or website.
From Latin 'pagina,' both kept the written surface meaning.

route = a road or path taken to reach a destination.
From Latin 'rupta via' (broken path, a road cleared through terrain), both describe a travel way.

président = the head of state, company, or organization.
From Latin 'praesidens' (sitting before, presiding), both name the person in charge.

lunettes (FR) = glasses for seeing better.
lunatic (EN) = a crazy or insane person.
French means glasses; English means a crazy person.

bibliothèque (FR) = a library, a place where you borrow books.
bibliography (EN) = a list of books or sources cited in a work.
Building in French; list in English.

forfait (FR) = a flat-rate package like a phone plan or ski pass.
forfeit (EN) = to lose something as a penalty.
French sells packages; English takes them away.

rapport (FR) = a written report or official account.
rapport (EN) = a relationship of trust or harmony.
French writes reports; English builds connections.

buffet (FR) = a self-service meal where people serve themselves.
buffet (EN) = the same: a self-service meal.
The word can also mean a sideboard or dining-room cabinet in both languages.

guitare = a stringed instrument played by plucking or strumming.
The word travelled from Arabic 'qitara' through Spanish and French to English, unchanged in meaning.

migration = the movement of people, animals, or data from one place to another.
From Latin 'migrare' (to move), both describe the same displacement.

cinéma = a movie theatre, or the film industry as a whole.
Short for 'cinématographe,' invented by the Lumière brothers in Lyon in 1895.

catastrophe = a sudden, large-scale disaster with severe consequences.
In Greek drama, 'katastrophe' was the final turning point of a play; the meaning shifted from endings to disasters.

tunnel = an underground or underwater passage.
From Old French 'tonnelle' (barrel vault), both describe the same enclosed corridor.

brillant = extremely intelligent, or shining with bright light.
From Italian 'brillare' (to sparkle), both kept the dual meaning of shine and intellect.

esprit (FR) = mind, intellect, or attitude.
spirit (EN) = a ghost, strong attitude, or alcohol.
French thinks; English haunts or drinks.

gentil (FR) = kind, nice, friendly.
gentle (EN) = soft, mild, not rough.
French is kind; English is gentle.

slip (FR) = briefs or underwear.
slip (EN) = to slide or make a mistake.
French puts it on; English loses balance.

caractère (FR) = personality or temperament.
character (EN) = a fictional person or someone's qualities.
French describes temperament; English can enter the story.

volcan = a mountain with an opening through which lava and gases erupt.
Named after Vulcanus, the Roman god of fire and metalworking.

horizon = the line where earth and sky appear to meet.
From Greek 'horizein' (to limit), both describe the same visual boundary.

décembre = the twelfth and final month of the year.
From Latin 'decem' (ten): it was the tenth month in the old Roman calendar before January and February were added.

guide = a person who leads others, or a book with useful information about a topic.
From Old French, both describe someone or something that shows the way.

collection = a group of gathered objects.
In fashion, it also refers to a designer's seasonal range of clothing; a usage shared by both languages.

liège (FR) = cork, the bark used for bottle stoppers.
liege (EN) = a feudal lord or sovereign.
French seals bottles; English rules vassals.

bride (FR) = a bridle, the straps used to control a horse.
bride (EN) = a woman getting married.
Reins vs. rings: no shared root despite identical spelling.

surnom (FR) = a nickname, an informal name from friends or family.
surname (EN) = a family name or last name.
Casual vs. official, despite the shared 'sur-' (over/above) prefix.

bague (FR) = a ring worn on a finger.
bag (EN) = a container used to carry items.
French wears rings; English carries bags.

dot (FR) = a dowry brought to marriage.
dot (EN) = a small round point.
French means a dowry; English means a small point.

festival = a large public event centred on music, film, or culture.
From Latin 'festivalis,' both name the same joyful public gatherings.

promotion (FR) = a career advancement or a marketing campaign; in universities, it can also mean a graduating class.
promotion (EN) = a career advancement or a marketing campaign.

ambulance = an emergency vehicle that transports patients to hospital.
From French 'hôpital ambulant' (mobile hospital), the word was born on Napoleonic battlefields.

latitude = a geographic coordinate showing how far north or south a place is.
Same meaning in both languages.

saxophone = a woodwind instrument with a brass body.
Named after Belgian inventor Adolphe Sax, who patented it in Paris in 1846.

compréhensif (FR) = understanding or sympathetic toward someone.
comprehensive (EN) = complete, broad, or covering everything.
French is about empathy; English is about coverage.

entendre (FR) = to hear, or sometimes to mean.
intend (EN) = to plan or mean to do something.
French hears; English plans.

sensitif (FR) = linked to the senses or sensory perception.
sensitive (EN) = easily affected, delicate, or emotionally responsive.
French is sensory; English is sensitivity.

avertissement (FR) = a warning or notice of danger.
advertisement (EN) = a paid ad or promotion.
French warns; English advertises.

commodité (FR) = convenience, comfort, or amenities.
commodity (EN) = a product, raw material, or tradable good.
French is convenience; English is merchandise.

convenance (FR) = propriety, suitability, or social appropriateness.
convenience (EN) = practical ease or usefulness.
French fits social rules; English makes life easier.

nouvelle (FR) = a short story or a piece of news.
novel (EN) = a long work of fiction.
French can be short fiction; English is a full book.

contrôler (FR) = to check, inspect, or verify.
control (EN) = to direct, command, or have power over something.
French often checks; English usually commands.

achever (FR) = to finish, complete, or kill.
achieve (EN) = to succeed in reaching a goal.
French finishes; English succeeds.

altérer (FR) = to spoil, damage, distort, or change for the worse.
alter (EN) = to change or modify.
French often damages; English simply changes.

grippe (FR) = the flu.
grip (EN) = a firm hold or grasp.
French is illness; English is holding.

plume (FR) = a feather, or a pen in some contexts.
plum (EN) = a plum fruit.
French writes or flies; English is fruit.

formel (FR) = clear, explicit, categorical, or definite.
formal (EN) = official, ceremonial, or not casual.
French is often categorical; English is often official.

défini (FR) = defined or specified.
definite (EN) = certain, clear, or without doubt.
French marks definition; English marks certainty.

délayer (FR) = to dilute or thin something with liquid.
delay (EN) = to make something late.
French adds liquid; English loses time.

conducteur (FR) = a driver, or something that conducts energy.
conductor (EN) = a person leading an orchestra or collecting fares.
French is usually the driver; English is often the orchestra leader.

large (FR) = wide or broad.
large (EN) = big in size or amount.
French is width; English is size.

abuser (FR) = to take advantage of, mislead, or overuse.
abuse (EN) = to mistreat, insult, or misuse.
The overlap is limited; the everyday meanings do not line up cleanly.

introduire (FR) = to insert or bring something in.
introduce (EN) = to present someone or something for the first time.
French often inserts; English often presents.

sentence (FR) = a court judgment or a formal maxim.
sentence (EN) = a complete grammatical unit of words.
French is legal or moral; English is grammar.

procéder (FR) = to carry out, act, or come from.
proceed (EN) = to continue or move forward.
French is method; English is movement or continuation.

notice (FR) = instructions or a user leaflet.
notice (EN) = a warning, announcement, or attention.
French explains how to use something; English catches attention.

annoter (FR) = to annotate or add written comments.
note (EN) = to notice, record, or mention.
French adds notes to a text; English can simply notice.

taper (FR) = to hit, type, or strike.
tap (EN) = to touch lightly or draw from a source.
French hits or types; English taps lightly.

faculté (FR) = an ability, or a university department.
faculty (EN) = teaching staff in a school or university.
French can mean ability or department; English usually means staff.

lecteur (FR) = a reader, or a media player.
lecturer (EN) = a university teacher who gives lectures.
French reads; English teaches.

pavé (FR) = a paving stone or cobblestone.
pavement (EN) = a sidewalk in UK English, or a road surface in US English.
French is the stone; English is the surface.

adapter (FR) = to adapt, adjust, or make something fit.
adopt (EN) = to take someone or something as one's own.
Trap: adapter matches adapt, not adopt.

adéquat (FR) = appropriate or suitable.
adequate (EN) = acceptable but not especially good.
French is suitable; English can sound merely sufficient.

affaire (FR) = a business, matter, deal, or case.
affair (EN) = a romantic relationship, scandal, or public matter.
French is often business; English often suggests scandal or romance.

agressif (FR) = hostile or violent.
aggressive (EN) = assertive, forceful, or sometimes hostile.
French is more negative; English can be positive in business.

agonie (FR) = death throes or the final stage before death.
agony (EN) = extreme pain or anguish.
French is dying; English is pain.

aliéné (FR) = mentally ill in older usage, or transferred away in legal language.
alien (EN) = foreign, strange, or extraterrestrial.
French is not the usual word for an extraterrestrial.

appointer (FR) = to pay a salary in older or formal usage.
appoint (EN) = to name someone to a role or fix a time.
French pays; English names or schedules.

appointements (FR) = salary or wages in formal French.
appointments (EN) = meetings or scheduled arrangements.
French pays people; English puts meetings in a calendar.

publicité (FR) = advertising, an advert, or a commercial.
publicity (EN) = public attention or media coverage.
French buys attention; English receives attention.

assistance (FR) = an audience, attendance, or help.
assistance (EN) = help or support.
French can mean the people present; English mainly means help.

audience (FR) = a hearing, interview, or court session.
audience (EN) = the people watching or listening.
French can be legal; English is usually the public.

balance (FR) = scales used for weighing.
balance (EN) = equilibrium, account balance, or weighing scales.
French usually weighs; English usually means equilibrium.

balancer (FR) = to swing, throw, or leak information.
balance (EN) = to keep steady or compare sides.
French can throw; English keeps things even.

balle (FR) = a small ball, bullet, or bale.
ball (EN) = a round object used in games.
French can be a bullet; English is usually a game ball.

baraque (FR) = a shack, hut, or informal house.
barrack (EN) = a military building where soldiers live.
French is an informal building; English is military housing.

bénéfice (FR) = profit or gain.
benefit (EN) = an advantage, payment, or help received.
French is often profit; English is often advantage.

bilan (FR) = an assessment, balance sheet, or toll.
bill (EN) = an invoice, banknote, or proposed law.
French sums up; English asks for payment.

blouse (FR) = a lab coat, work coat, or smock.
blouse (EN) = a woman's shirt.
French is often professional clothing; English is a top.

bond (FR) = a leap or jump.
bond (EN) = a connection, obligation, or financial security.
French jumps; English connects or finances.

bonnet (FR) = a beanie, cap, or bra cup.
bonnet (EN) = a baby hat or a car hood in UK English.
French is everyday headwear; English is narrower.

brocanteur (FR) = a secondhand dealer.
broker (EN) = a person who arranges deals, insurance, or investments.
French sells old goods; English brokers deals.

bureau (FR) = an office, desk, or department.
bureau (EN) = a chest of drawers or an agency.
French is where you work; English can be furniture.

cabinet (FR) = a practice, office, small room, or restroom in some contexts.
cabinet (EN) = a cupboard or a group of senior ministers.
French often means a professional office; English often means furniture or government.

cachet (FR) = a stamp, seal, tablet, or performer's fee.
cachet (EN) = prestige or a mark of distinction.
French can be a pill or fee; English is prestige.

cadre (FR) = a frame, setting, or executive.
cadre (EN) = a small group of trained activists or leaders.
French frames things or manages; English names a core group.

camisole (FR) = mainly seen in camisole de force, a straitjacket.
camisole (EN) = a light sleeveless top.
French restrains; English is clothing.

campagne (FR) = the countryside, or a campaign.
campaign (EN) = a planned political, military, or marketing effort.
French can mean rural land; English is organized action.

canapé (FR) = a sofa or couch.
canape (EN) = a small appetizer on bread or pastry.
French sits down; English serves a bite.

cap (FR) = a course, cape, milestone, or threshold.
cap (EN) = a hat, lid, or limit.
French points direction; English covers or limits.

caprice (FR) = a whim or tantrum.
caprice (EN) = a sudden fancy or impulsive change.
French is often childish; English is more literary.

carton (FR) = cardboard, a box, or a big success in slang.
carton (EN) = a milk or juice container, or a box.
French is the material or box; English is usually the container.

censure (FR) = censorship.
censure (EN) = strong official criticism.
French suppresses speech; English criticizes officially.

cerise (FR) = a cherry.
cerise (EN) = a bright cherry-red color.
French is fruit; English is mainly a color word.

change (FR) = currency exchange.
change (EN) = change, alteration, or coins.
French exchanges money; English changes things.

chant (FR) = singing or a song.
chant (EN) = a repeated slogan, call, or simple religious song.
French is singing; English is repetition.

chantier (FR) = a construction site or messy project.
shanty (EN) = a rough hut or sea song.
French builds; English shelters or sings.

chapeau (FR) = a hat, or an introductory heading.
chapeau (EN) = a hat, especially in a French cultural context.
French is everyday; English is rare and borrowed.

chèque (FR) = a cheque or payment document.
check (EN) = a verification, mark, or bill in US restaurants.
French pays; English checks.

chiffon (FR) = a rag or cleaning cloth.
chiffon (EN) = a light, transparent fabric.
French cleans; English dresses.

chiffre (FR) = a digit, figure, or numerical code.
cipher (EN) = a secret code or a zero-like symbol.
French counts; English hides information.

cité (FR) = an estate, housing project, or ancient city.
city (EN) = a large town or urban area.
French can mean housing estate; English is the whole city.

baskets (FR) = sneakers or trainers.
baskets (EN) = containers used for carrying or holding things.
French goes on your feet; English holds objects.

clerc (FR) = a notary's assistant or cleric in some contexts.
clerk (EN) = an office or shop employee.
French is more specialized; English is a general employee.

clinique (FR) = a private hospital or clinic.
clinic (EN) = an outpatient medical center or specialist service.
French can mean a private hospital; English is usually a consultation center.

coche (FR) = a tick mark or old coach.
coach (EN) = a trainer, bus, or carriage.
French marks a box; English trains people.

colis (FR) = a parcel or package.
collision (EN) = a crash between moving things.
French delivers; English crashes.

commande (FR) = an order for goods, or a control.
command (EN) = an instruction, command, or authority.
French buys or controls; English orders people.

commentaire (FR) = a comment, note, or commentary.
comment (EN) = a remark or response.
French can be a full analytical commentary; English is often a short remark.

commercial (FR) = sales-related, or a salesperson as a noun.
commercial (EN) = an advertisement, or related to commerce.
French names the sales role; English often means an ad.

commis (FR) = a clerk, assistant, or junior worker.
committee (EN) = a group appointed to handle a task.
French is one person; English is a group.

commode (FR) = a chest of drawers, or convenient as an adjective.
commodious (EN) = spacious and roomy.
French can be furniture; English means roomy.

compagnie (FR) = companionship, guests, or a company.
company (EN) = a business or group of people.
French can mean keeping someone company; English is usually a business or group.

complet (FR) = a suit, or full as an adjective.
complete (EN) = finished, whole, or entire.
French can be clothing; English is completion.

compléter (FR) = to add what is missing or fill in.
complete (EN) = to finish or make whole.
French often adds to; English often finishes.

complexion (FR) = constitution or overall health in older or formal French.
complexion (EN) = skin tone or facial appearance.
French is constitution; English is skin tone.

compliment (FR) = praise or a polite remark.
complement (EN) = something that completes or goes well with something else.
French praises; English completes.

composant (FR) = a component or part.
composer (EN) = a person who writes music.
French is a part; English is a person.

compromis (FR) = a compromise, or a property sale agreement.
compromise (EN) = an agreement after concessions, or damage to integrity.
French can be a sales agreement; English is the concession itself.

compromission (FR) = a shady deal or discreditable involvement.
compromise (EN) = an agreement or a weakening of standards.
French suggests discredit; English can be neutral.

compulsion (FR) = constraint or obligation from outside.
compulsion (EN) = an irresistible internal urge.
French is external pressure; English is internal urge.

compte (FR) = an account, bill, count, or story.
count (EN) = a number count, or a noble title when capitalized.
French manages an account; English counts.

contrôleur (FR) = an inspector or ticket collector.
controller (EN) = a device, regulator, or financial officer.
French checks tickets; English controls systems.

break (FR) = a station wagon in French car vocabulary.
break (EN) = a pause, split, or interruption.
French can be a car; English is a pause.

smoking (FR) = a tuxedo or dinner jacket.
smoking (EN) = the act of smoking tobacco.
French dresses up; English lights up.

dressing (FR) = a walk-in closet or wardrobe area.
dressing (EN) = salad sauce or a medical bandage.
French stores clothes; English dresses salad or wounds.

relooking (FR) = a makeover or style change.
relooking (EN) = not a standard English word in this sense.
French uses a pseudo-English word; English says makeover.

footing (FR) = jogging or a run.
footing (EN) = a base, foundation, or financial standing.
French runs; English stands on a base.

zapping (FR) = channel-hopping on television.
zapping (EN) = not the usual English word for changing channels.
French flips channels; English says channel-hopping.

planning (FR) = a schedule or timetable.
planning (EN) = the act or process of making plans.
French is the timetable; English is the process.

sweat (FR) = a sweatshirt.
sweat (EN) = perspiration.
French wears it; English produces it.

self (FR) = a cafeteria or self-service restaurant.
self (EN) = one's own person or identity.
French eats there; English talks about identity.

forcing (FR) = strong pressure or a push to make something happen.
forcing (EN) = the act of making someone do something, or a technical term in sport or computing.
French uses pseudo-English for pressure; English uses a different structure.

tennisman (FR) = a tennis player in French everyday speech.
tennisman (EN) = not the standard English word for a tennis player.
French uses tennisman; English says tennis player.

A small ending shift: French automatiser becomes English automate. Same meaning: make a task run automatically.

adapter (FR) = to adapt, adjust, or make something fit.
adapt (EN) = to change something so it fits a new need.
Safe match: adapter matches adapt; do not confuse it with adopt.
Same spelling and same meaning. It works for adopting a child, but also for adopting a new technology, tool, or strategy.

A central teamwork word. Same spelling and same meaning: working together on a shared project or goal.

The accents disappear in English, but the meaning stays the same. Decision is a core business word for choosing between options.
The initial accent disappears in English. Same meaning: an assessment, review, or evaluation, including annual performance evaluations.

The accent disappears in English, but the meaning stays the same: a choice made from several options.

Same meaning for eyesight and long-term strategy. In business English, vision often means the direction a leader wants to build toward.
Same spelling and same meaning: a task, purpose, or company direction. Mission statement is a common business phrase.

Same spelling and same meaning, but often slightly more formal in English: a serious exchange of ideas or points of view.

Same spelling and same meaning. Useful for physical equipment, software setup, and technical deployment.

Same spelling and same meaning. It can describe speaking in a meeting or a technical visit by an engineer on site.
A perfect true friend for restrictions, technical constraints, or legal limits. English stress falls near the end: lim-i-TAY-shun.
Same spelling, but English business usage often means onboarding or initial training for a new employee.
Perfectly transparent. Same meaning: taking part in an activity, meeting, project, or decision process.
The accent disappears in English. Same professional meaning: a talk, deck, or meeting presentation.
The accent disappears in English. Same meaning: an emotional, physical, chemical, or user reaction.
Very close, but watch the middle: French recommandation becomes English recommendation. Same meaning: advice or a formal suggestion.
The accent disappears in English. Same meaning: making something smaller or lower, such as cost reduction or risk reduction.
The accent disappears in English. Same meaning: official rules, legal control, or automatic control of a system.
A perfect written twin. Common in aviation, finance, medicine, training, and video games.
A perfect written twin. In English, the ending sounds like -cher: STRUK-cher. Useful for company structure, code structure, and document structure.
French -gie becomes English -gy, and the accent disappears. English stresses the first syllable: STRAT-uh-jee.

French processus becomes the shorter English process. Essential for describing the steps, workflow, or sequence of a project.

A clean true friend. It works for document size, file type (.pdf, .csv), media format, or meeting structure.
French profil becomes English profile, with a final silent -e. Useful for a user account, a social media page, or a candidate description.

French -té becomes English -ty. Capacity can mean maximum volume, production ability, storage space, or legal ability.
French -té becomes English -ty. A daily management word for what should be handled first.
Another -té to -ty pattern. Quality can mean product excellence, quality control, or a positive personal trait.
French -té becomes English -ty, and the French accent disappears. Security works for physical safety, road safety, IT security, and cybersecurity.
French -té becomes English -ty. Stability is used for an economy, an infrastructure, a relationship, or reliable software.
French -té becomes English -ty. In modern business English, visibility means clear access to data, progress, risks, or forecasts.

French -té becomes English -ty. Diversity is a major workplace concept in modern company culture.
French -té becomes English -ty. Identity works for official documents and for tech, especially identity and access management.

French -isme becomes English -ism, and the accent disappears. Realism means seeing or representing things as they are.
